The commercial resiliency of alt-metal and post-grunge really is astonishing. After all, many of the biggest hits of the 2010s came from veteran hard rockers (Disturbed, Three Days Grace, Breaking Benjamin) rooted in these ’90s subgenres. Exceptions emerged, of course. While Greta Van Fleet’s Led Zeppelin-inspired rave-ups and Ghost’s doom-metal nightmares may seem, at first blush, radically different from each other, the success of both reflected the growing number of young acts revisiting ’70s metal. Even Denmark’s Volbeat, around since the mid-2000s, finally broke in the United States thanks largely to their classic metal riffs. The mainstreaming of metalcore and hardcore also warrants mentioning: Bring Me the Horizon and A Day to Remember gradually attained stardom thanks to their knack for mixing furious breakdowns with sparkling pop productions. It represented a genuinely fresh twist and perhaps a sign of future developments for hard rock.

A-List Pop is home to the latest and greatest in the world of pop music. At the top of this week’s playlist is Olivia Rodrigo’s “obsessed” from the just-released deluxe version of her sophomore album, GUTS (spilled). Check back often, as our editors update this playlist regularly—and if you hear something you like, add it to your library.

One of the most distinctive male voices of contemporary Bollywood, Arijit Singh brings an intimate, husky timbre to breezy acoustic-driven pop and swelling, cinematic numbers marked by romantic strings and ethereal synths. While the playback singer's wheelhouse is the soul-stirring love ballad that marks many a heartfelt movie moment, Singh is a versatile performer who's as adept at poetic paeans as he is club thumpers, boisterous bhangra tracks, Punjabi folk and Arabic pop flavoured with his memorable vibrato.
Dan the man ka tribute to Avicii

Melodies that gleam like festival lights, floor-shaking drops, sublime vocal hooks—Avicii was a master of hands-in-the-air EDM anthems. His music cuts between arena-scale house epics, hypnotic trance bangers and crossover dance-pop smashes with the crowd-pumping skill of a killer DJ. Despite his undeniable club credentials, there's way more to the Swedish DJ-producer's sound than thumping beats and rumbling basslines. Blending sparkling synth riffs with pulsing rhythms, Avicii classics like “Levels” deliver an instant, ecstatic hit of pure pleasure, and helped set off the EDM explosion of the early '10s. But his genre-smashing tracks like “Wake Me Up”, which mashed up EDM with bluegrass and soul, go beyond mere body-moving thrills—they're bold experiments that helped introduce genuine songwriting and a spectrum of new sounds to dance music.

K-pop quartet BLACKPINK mix elements of rap into their pop to craft brash, booming songs. They crashed into the Korean music scene in 2016 with the uptempo electro cut “BOOMBAYAH” and the more unnerving chug of “WHISTLE”. Since then, they've gradually incorporated other styles into their music. They deliver swaggering verses above hard-hitting beats (“DDU-DU DDU-DU”) and venture into heartfelt balladry over acoustic guitar (“STAY”). They've worked with Western acts like Dua Lipa, creating shuffling dance pop playing off one another's strengths, and it's unique collaborations like this that highlight their ascendance outside Korea.

Whether a comedy or a drama, the music and voices of Bollywood films have always had their constants: a desire to move the feet and the soul, and a drive to change with the times. These instant classics of the 20th and 21st centuries bolster traditional Sufi devotionals and bhangra dance breaks with Western instrumentals and classical flourishes. Alongside these powerful fusions are songs influenced by international pop and hip-hop, befitting India's ties with both its own medley of cultures and its diaspora.

Bollywood songs have an unmistakable sense of language and melody. From intricate, metaphor-heavy poetry to charged-up electronic beats mashed with folk rhythms, these numbers elevate the mood of films across the industry. Our collection of Bollywood Hits is updated regularly. If you hear something you like, add it to your library.

Dance music moves at the speed of light, so here's your telescope: These are the everybody-on-the-floor bangers, crucial IDs and innovative sounds making waves in clubs, warehouses and festivals worldwide. Fresh styles from up-and-coming artists and bold new moves from some of the biggest in the scene: If everyone isn't talking about these songs today, they will be tomorrow. Our editors regularly refresh this playlist. If you like a track, add it to your library.

BTS aren’t your typical K-pop boy band: These guys prefer sexy slow jams to mushy ballads, and rap to pretty much anything else. Their songs come in just about every flavour of hip-hop, from thrashy rap-rock to classic G-funk. While they’re best known for rhyming about social issues affecting youth, they also bring the same level of passion and wordplay to talking about relationships or just having a good time.

Cuban-born Camila Cabello fired up the pop world in 2017 with “Havana”, a midtempo, piano-led lament that paired its longing with an irresistibly sultry groove. The former Fifth Harmony member's career has been defined by its versatility—she lords over thudding EDM on “Crying in the Club” and melts into the strummy acousti-pop of her Shawn Mendes collab “I Know What You Did Last Summer”. Cabello's wide vocal range makes her an enticing foil for MCs and DJs alike; collaborators such as the fast-talking rapper Machine Gun Kelly and the turntablist Cashmere Cat use her stunning soprano to complement their own styles.

Though born with perfect pitch, this New Jersey native has been doggedly honing his craft since age four, when he began learning classical piano—and set off on the journey of getting closer to expressing the perfect convergence of modern pop and timeless R&B. The cleancut Berklee School of Music grad who emerged in 2015 with emotionally exposed ballads like Paul Walker tribute "See You Again" and peppy malt-shop bops like "Marvin Gaye" quickly grew into a bona fide soul man and maestro. To wit, he swoons in harmony with throwback greats Boyz II Men on the same album—his second, 2018's Voicenotes—that finds him smouldering alongside futurist Kehlani.

Coldplay articulate the moments and emotions that often seem indefinable—that euphoric high of falling in love, the gut-wrenching pain of falling out of it, the potent buzz of collective hope. It all starts with Chris Martin's sincerity and introspection—he's as likely to reflect and lament as to look outward—and a falsetto that absolutely soars. The band is right alongside him, carrying soft piano-and-guitar rock to heart-racing crescendos, and experimenting, over the years, with orchestral arrangements, moody electronics and producers like Brian Eno.

It’s not just that Eminem is offensive—he’d rap about killing his mom for a good punchline (and has). It’s that in the process of deliberately trying to piss off everyone within reach, he's managed to tap into the American id with a clarity most artists—rappers or otherwise—don’t have the mettle to. And like any comedian worth his props, he never lets you get a laugh off without forcing you to think about about the tragedies that forged it. From provocations and murder fantasies to gut-turning examinations of his own traumas and travails, here’s the best of Eminem—a definitive artist of his era.

Galantis' effortless blend of pop and dance is second nature: Christian Karlsson, also a member of indie electro-poppers Miike Snow, has written for Madonna and Katy Perry; DJ Linus Eklöw, a.k.a. Style of Eye, co-wrote Icona Pop's "I Love It". Together, the Swedish duo put their diverse talents to good use in songs that pair giddy choruses and colourful arrangements with the pizzazz of EDM's production. The results sound vintage, modern and timeless all at once—a riot of kazoos, snare rolls and children's voices, but their confetti-cannon rush is tempered by exquisitely melancholy undertones.

Green Day started out as a scrappy, melodic punk band in the late '80s, slowly building a cult audience thanks to a string of indie albums full of caffeinated riffs and catchy hooks. In 1994, they had an unexpected multi-platinum smash with their third album, Dookie, and over the decades that followed, became the godfathers of modern pop-punk, inspiring countless bands. Green Day also grew increasingly ambitious, releasing the critically acclaimed concept album American Idiot in 2004, but they never lost the sarcastic, relatable edge that first made them underground heroes.

There's nothing wrong with taking a little me-time. Close the door, find a comfy corner and get in your feelings with these moody, downtempo pop tunes. We update this playlist regularly. If you like a track, add it to your library.

This classical crossover star sways listeners with his smooth voice, but he's more than a tenor with a wide range. Groban's vocal dexterity is matched by his instrumental skills, as he can play both piano and percussion parts. Starting with his self-titled 2001 debut, he has demonstrated an ability to fuse adult contemporary pop styles with the textures of opera, making new compositions sound modern yet stately. He's charmed audiences by collaborating with jazz pianist Herbie Hancock and Broadway star Audra McDonald, bridging musical universes with his accessible, buttoned-up pop.

Kygo's ascent is the stuff of legend: in no time, the Norwegian producer went from making bootleg remixes of Ed Sheeran and Marvin Gaye to getting tapped to replace Avicii on TomorrowWorld's main stage. In the process, he softened EDM's profile, trading builds and drops for floating on air. Given his balmy atmospheres and easy grooves, he's often associated with tropical house, but Kygo's music can't be pinned down to any one style. Equally suited for beach bonfires, after-parties and road trips, it's the soundtrack for life's most delicious stretches of downtime.

LINKIN PARK helped write the nu-metal playbook, then proceeded to tear it up. Their 2000 debut, Hybrid Theory, is a genre milestone, what with its tormented pleas, brooding rhymes and crunchy breakdowns all plastered together with dense sampling and scratching. The band has since made intrepid forays into cyborg-like pummel infused with dubstep bass drops, as well as atmospheric hybrids of alt-rock and gauzy electronic music. Proving that youth is only a state of mind, The Hunting Party, released in 2014, found the veterans revisiting the blitzing hardcore of their teens.

When Maroon 5 released their debut, Songs About Jane, in 2002, it was truly novel. Radio was riding out the boy-band explosion, dirge-y modern rock was ubiquitous and hip-hop hadn’t quite taken over the mainstream. Fronted by the clean-cut Adam Levine, a suave crooner with a supple voice, the group served up unabashedly tender soft-rock tunes with nods to Stevie Wonder and Michael Jackson. It was a winning formula: They were soon pop mainstays, ramping up the allure of their agile jams with racy lyrics, a shot of electro-funk, overt nods to Prince and, of course, “Moves Like Jagger”.

What's airy as spun sugar and contains all the colours of the rainbow? That'd be the music of Marshmello, a mysterious producer who, hidden behind his white marshmallow mask—inspiring many fan theories about his identity—arrived in 2015 with the sweetest, fluffiest EDM imaginable. Marrying neon-streaked trance stabs to trunk-rattling trap beats, his music offers the perfect merger of melody, main-stage intensity and emotional payoff. He's got range too: The blindingly bright "Find Me" juggles future house with Jersey club, while "Ritual" slows down to indulge in slinky tropical house bliss.

Rising out of India's electronic scene, Udyan Sagar—a.k.a Nucleya—started out as the frontman of the experimental Bandish Projekt in 1998. His solo work has seen him build on that pioneering spirit, infusing South Asian street and folk music with his signature bass-heavy sound. One of India's first proponents of dubstep, Nucleya uses the underlying aggression of bass and the temperance of simple, half-time drums as rough-edged textures to fuel his power-packed performances across the country.

There's nothing like a little music to keep the workplace humming. This uptempo, easygoing playlist—covering the best in recent pop, dance, hip-hop, R&B and more—is designed to carry you through from 9 to 5. We regularly update these tunes. If you hear something you like, add it to your library.

Legend has it Simon Cowell only took 10 minutes to decide to bring then-teenaged contestants Harry Styles, Niall Horan, Zayn Malik, Louis Tomlinson and Liam Payne together to form a boy band on The X Factor in July 2010. And yet, no one could’ve predicted what would follow. One Direction became total global superstars with ubiquitous pop-rock hits—from the playful power pop of 2011’s “What Makes You Beautiful”, the group’s first single, to the rootsy “History” in 2015, the group’s last. In their short five-year career, One Direction became the biggest act on the planet all while challenging traditional boy-band tropes. They didn’t dance. They had tattoos. They co-wrote their songs. They traversed a multitude of musical territories, from the bubblegum of “Live While We’re Young” and “Best Song Ever” (a modern-day “Baba O’Riley”) and the midtempo folk balladry of “Little Things” to the 1980s piano rock of “Steal My Girl” and the serotonin-releasing, pitch-perfect harmonies of, well, their entire discography. Dive in here.

Flirting with pop, rock, folk, funk, R&B, even classical music, this Colorado band offers one notable constant: an undeniably killer hook. Oh, and drama—plenty of it. It's all built on Ryan Tedder's soulful croons, which fluctuate with every passing mood, as he quivers through jilted pain on the cello-touched piano ballad "Apologize", unleashes a slick falsetto over the sweeping synth-pop of "Kids", and rhythmically rivals the rousing, hand-clapping folk of "Counting Stars". But OneRepublic's greatest triumph? That just might be bringing Bach to stadiums worldwide with pop anthem "Secrets".

There’s nothing like the sound of a piano alone. Intimate, ruminative and relaxed, this mix highlights the sound of solo piano in repose: calm, in 88 keys. Our editors rotate selections regularly, so if you hear something you like, add it to your library.

There’s no pick-me-up as profound—or profoundly simple—as exercise. It’s not just that your body’s built for it; it’s the pride and satisfaction that comes from getting out and moving in the face of the distractions that might otherwise hold you back. The tracks here aren’t bound by style or era, but they share an energy and sense of optimism that make great companions for whatever workout you might be tackling, from weights at the gym to walks in the woods. So long as you’re moving, you’re good. Our editors update picks here regularly, so if you hear something you like, take a second and add it to your library.

When the biggest stars of pop and EDM need a soaring hook, they call Ryan Tedder. Fronting OneRepublic made him famous, but this mix of collaborations, co-writes and songs for other musicians shows that every track Tedder touches is destined for greatness.

Dutch-born DJ and producer San Holo has his head in the stars. You could probably guess as much from his Millennium Falcon-worthy name, but his style comes through even stronger in his tracks, which tackle EDM and future bass with a whimsical, neon-hued sense of wonder. His 2016 single “Light” sounds downright wide-eyed with its lilting vocal loop and massive candy-floss synthesisers, while on “The Future”, a team-up with James Vincent McMorrow, San Holo uses the indie folkster's crooning voice to create a moody R&B banger as luminescent and enveloping as the night sky.

Canadian troubadour Shawn Mendes' teen-idol appeal and soulful voice helped him become a social-media star in the mid-2010s. His debut single, “Life of the Party”, is a sweeping piano ballad that shows off his passionate vocals, and the hits that followed—like the wounded “Stitches”—combine thoughtful lyrics with insistent rhythms. The galloping “There's Nothing Holdin' Me Back” and the longing “Treat You Better”, both of which Mendes co-wrote, have a youthful bounce that underscores their lyrics' urgency; the slinky “Lost in Japan” strips down and foregrounds its bouncing-ball bassline, allowing Mendes to shift into international-lover mode.

Like the idea of the teenager, the definition of “teen pop” is always changing—just ask now-grown bobby-soxers, Beatlemaniacs and Backstreet fans. But at its core, it’s always been synonymous with hooky songs that chronicled heartbreak, soundtracked dance crazes and let adolescents blow off steam. The 2020s’ embrace of video-sharing sites accelerated the pace of teen pop’s evolution, with pop-punk and emo-rap just two of the styles that dominated trending charts. But the emotions expressed in song by the likes of Olivia Rodrigo, Billie Eilish and Tate McRae are timeless.

Music gives us so much—an escape, a salve, a reflection of the world in which we live. But in 2020, it felt vital in a new way. Consider the joys of Dua Lipa’s “Break My Heart”, a modern, disco-indebted stunner that—outside of the countless clubs and parties for which it’s still destined—reminded us to keep dancing, especially in quarantine. Or the courage of Lil Baby, who, in the midst of a global reckoning with systemic racism, drew on his own personal experiences for “The Bigger Picture”, a civil rights anthem for a new generation of protestors. From Bad Bunny to Bieber, Roddy Ricch to Morgan Wallen and The Weeknd, music of all styles and perspectives brought us closer together at a time when many of us have been forced apart. That’s the story of the year, and these are the songs and sounds that defined it, as chosen by Apple Music’s team of editors.

This UK foursome are true kids of the internet: they formed online, and first came to fame through their hugely popular YouTube covers of artists including One Direction, Taylor Swift and P!NK. Though they've shied away from the “boy band” tag—keen to point out that they're their own men and all play instruments—their shiny, high-energy songs bounce around in the middle ground between 1D and the pop-punk likes of Busted or, indeed, The Vamps' former tourmates McFly. They might not suck your blood, but they will win the hardest of hearts.

This duo exploded into a '10s pop phenomenon with their omnivorous musical tastes and relatable emotional vulnerability. On "Stressed Out", the pilots mix sinewy hip-hop beats with Tyler Joseph's stream-of-consciousness rhymes, adding up to a snappy, laidback tongue twister. “Holding On To You", meanwhile, is a piano-spackled emo crooner that swings between soulful, soaring melodies and urgently delivered raps. Regardless of whatever style they may be trying on, twenty one pilots pour their hearts into their music, whether they're singing about love ("Tear In My Heart") or spitting verses on existential anxiety ("Car Radio").
